title: Socrates Speaks
description: Take a first step into Classical Attic Greek through a line of Platonic dialogue.
context: In Plato's Euthyphro, Socrates meets Euthyphro near the court in Athens. Socrates is facing the charge brought against him by Meletus. The conversational form gives us short pieces of genuine Attic Greek.

grammar.title: The present plural
grammar.explanation: A Greek verb ending can identify its subject even before you have found the corresponding noun.

example.note: καλοῦσιν is third-person plural present active.

grammar.title: Addressing someone
grammar.explanation: The vocative is used when directly addressing someone. It frequently appears with ὦ.

example.note: English normally omits 'O' in ordinary translation.

grammar.title: Not this, but that
grammar.explanation: Greek frequently builds contrast with a negative expression followed by ἀλλά.

example.note: Look for the contrast before trying to translate every particle individually.

grammar.title: Small Greek particles
grammar.explanation: Words such as δή and γε add emphasis, connection or nuance. They do not always need an individual English word.

example.note: Read the phrase as a whole rather than forcing a separate English equivalent for every particle.

texts.title: Not an Action, but an Indictment
texts.greek: οὔτοι δὴ Ἀθηναῖοί γε, ὦ Εὐθύφρων, δίκην αὐτὴν καλοῦσιν ἀλλὰ γραφήν.
readingHints: ὦ Εὐθύφρων is direct address and stands outside the main sentence.
Look at δίκην and γραφήν together: both are accusative.
Use οὔ ... ἀλλά to build the basic structure: 'they do not call it X, but Y'.
texts.translation: The Athenians, Euthyphro, do not call it an action, but an indictment.
